Save or Scrap? 1976 Chevrolet Laguna S-3 Junkyard Find Still Has the Slanted NASCAR Nose
10 photos
Photo: Junkyard Life/YouTube
Introduced in 1964 as Chevrolet's first mid-size car, the Chevelle went on to become one of the brand's best-selling models, moving over seven million units through 1977. The Chevelle line also included the Malibu, which replaced it altogether in 1978, as well as the lesser-known Laguna.
Named after the iconic coastal community of California, the Malibu also debuted for the 1964 model year. It was the top-of-the-line trim level of the Chevelle until 1972. Relegated to mid-level duty in 1973, the Malibu badge returned on a range-topping model in 1974, this time around as the Malibu Classic.
It became a stand-alone model in 1978 until it was discontinued in 1983. The Malibu made a comeback in 1997, remaining in production all the way until 2025.
Named after the popular Laguna Beach, also located in California, the Chevelle Laguna debuted in 1973. It's the car that replaced the Malibu as the top-of-the-line model that year, but that changed the following year. While the 1973 Laguna was also available as a four-door sedan and station wagon, the 1974 version was restricted to the two-door coupe body style.
Now called the Laguna S-3, it became the performance option of the Chevelle line, replacing the discontinued SS model. In 1975, Chevrolet revised the S-3 with a slanted aero-style nose designed for NASCAR. That's because Chevrolet had been using the car on the oval tracks since 1973.
Raced for five seasons, the coupe scored a total of 53 wins, most of them in S-3 spec. These helped Chevrolet win no fewer than four manufacturers' championships. Cale Yarborough also won the first two of his three consecutive Winston Cup titles driving the Laguna. The nameplate was discontinued after NASCAR rendered the S-3 ineligible for competition following the 1977 season.
Outside the race track, the Laguna S-3 was far less successful than the regular Chevelle. The company sold 38,790 units from 1974 to 1976, with most of them delivered in the first year. This S-3 is one of only 9,100 examples built in 1976.
Sadly, this Laguna has spent most of its life off the road, most likely parked outside. It was recently discovered in a junkyard in Alabama in very rough condition. It's so rusty that the optional swivel seats are no longer attached to the floor. Speaking of options, this car was also ordered with a center console, air conditioning, and cruise control.
The engine is still under the hood, but the intake and carburetor are gone. Needless to say, this Laguna won't be running and driving anytime soon.
The S-3 was available with three engines in 1976, starting with a 305-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) V8 rated at 140 horsepower. Chevrolet also offered a 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) V8 in two- and four-barrel configurations (145 and 165 horsepower). The range-topping 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) big-block V8 came with 175 horsepower on tap.
Is this Laguna worth saving? Well, since these cars barely fetch over $15,000 when in excellent condition, a heavily damaged example will cost way too much to restore. This Chevy needs pretty much everything, so it will probably end up in the crusher. It's sad, but that's how the cookie crumbles more often than not.
